questions.stem: Look at the four parts of a function definition. Which part is **always required** even when the function takes no input?
questions.explanation: The return type is mandatory in every function definition (it can be `void`, but it must be written). The parameter list may be empty `()`, the `return` statement is only needed for non-void functions, and writing `void` inside the parentheses (C-style) is optional in C++.
Trace from the inside out. `f(g(3))`: `g(3) = 6`, then `f(6) = 7`. `g(f(3))`: `f(3) = 4`, then `g(4) = 8`. Output: `7 8`.

options.text: `cout` cannot print the return value of a function
`add` is called before it is declared or defined
The function `add` has the wrong return type
`main` must come after every other function

questions.explanation: C++ requires a function to be **declared** (via prototype) or **defined** before it is called. Adding `int add(int, int);` above `main` fixes the error. Note: `main` does not have to come last — placing the full definition of `add` above `main` would also work.

questions.stem: Which **single line** added at the top would make Q3's program compile?
questions.explanation: `int add(int, int);` is a valid function prototype. Parameter names are optional in a prototype — only the return type, name, and parameter *types* are required.

options.text: Compile error because of two `return` statements

questions.explanation: `n > 0` is true for `n = 5`, so the first `return 1;` executes immediately and the function exits. The other return statements are *unreachable code*. Multiple return statements are perfectly legal — only the first one reached executes.

options.text: The function never actually returns anything

questions.explanation: The lines `-x;` and `x;` are valid statements (they evaluate an expression and discard it), but the function never executes a `return`. The result is undefined behaviour. The fix: write `return -x;` and `return x;`.

questions.stem: Complete the prototype so the following call is legal: `float a = average(3, 4, 5);`
questions.explanation: The call passes three `int` arguments and assigns the result to a `float`, so the function must return `float` and accept three `int` parameters in order.
`inc` receives `n` by **value** (a copy of `x`). Modifying the copy has no effect on `x` in `main`, so `x` is still `5` after the call.

questions.stem: Modify Q8 so that `inc` actually changes `x` in `main`. Which signature works?
questions.explanation: `int& n` is a **reference parameter** — the function operates on the same memory cell as `x`, so any change persists after the call.
The swap function dereferences the pointers and exchanges the values stored at the addresses of `x` and `y`, so the final values are swapped.

questions.stem: Why does `swap(x, y);` (without `&`) **not** work for the swap function declared as `void swap(int *a, int *b)`?

options.text: Pointer parameters require addresses, not values
Pointers can only point to `const` data

questions.explanation: The function expects `int *` (a pointer), so the call must supply addresses (`&x`, `&y`). Passing `x` and `y` directly passes values, which the compiler will refuse because the types do not match.

questions.stem: Which statement about C++ references is **true**?

options.text: A reference can be reassigned to refer to a different object later
A reference variable must be initialised when declared
References can be `null`, just like pointers
References use the `*` operator to access the underlying value

questions.explanation: A reference must be bound to an object at the moment of declaration and cannot be re-bound afterwards. References cannot be null and do not need an explicit dereference operator.
Inner: `max(2,7) = 7`, `max(4,5) = 5`. Outer: `max(7, 5) = 7`. The ternary `(a > b) ? a : b` is a compact form of an if/else.

questions.stem: The function `int f(int n) { return n; }` is called as `f(3.7)`. What value is returned?
questions.explanation: Passing a `double` (3.7) to an `int` parameter triggers an implicit narrowing conversion that **truncates** the fractional part. The function receives `3` and returns `3`. (Some compilers warn about this conversion.)

questions.stem: Which is the **smallest valid** definition of a function that does nothing and returns nothing?
questions.explanation: `void nop() {}` is a complete, legal function: void return type, name, empty parameter list, empty body. Option A is also legal but adds an unnecessary `return;`. Option C lacks a return type. Option D is a *variable* declaration of type `void` (illegal).

options.text: The integer division truncates the decimal part
The parameters must be of type `float`

questions.explanation: `a + b` is `int`, and `2` is `int`, so `(a+b)/2` performs **integer division**. To get a true average, write `(a + b) / 2.0` to force floating-point division, or cast one operand to `float`.
The ternary operator `(condition) ? value_if_true : value_if_false` is the idiomatic single-expression way to choose between two values. Option D would be infinite recursion.
`3*3 + 4*4 = 9 + 16 = 25`. (This is the Pythagorean identity for a 3-4-5 right triangle.)

options.text: `greet` is missing parentheses, so it is not actually called

questions.explanation: Writing `greet;` only references the function but does not invoke it. The call must be `greet();`. This is a very common beginner mistake.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about pass-by-reference is **false**?

options.text: The function can modify the caller's variable
No copy of the argument is made, so it is faster for large objects
References must be initialised when they are first declared
Reference parameters always require the `&` operator at the call site

questions.explanation: The `&` is part of the **parameter declaration** (`void f(int& x)`), not the call site. The function is called as `f(y);` — the same syntax used for pass-by-value.
`triple(4) = 12`, then `triple(12) = 36`. Functions can be composed by passing the return value of one as the argument of another.

questions.stem: Write a one-line function body that returns whether an integer is **even**. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: An integer is even iff its remainder when divided by 2 is zero. Option A returns 0 or 1 (the remainder), not a clean boolean for *even*. Option C is true only when `-1 ≤ n ≤ 1`.

options.text: Prints garbage — the function returns no value when `n <= 0`

questions.explanation: The function only returns a value when `n > 0`. For `n = -3`, control falls off the end of a non-void function, which is **undefined behaviour**. The program may print 0, 1, garbage, or crash.

questions.stem: Which is the correct prototype declaration corresponding to the function definition `double area(double r) { return 3.14 * r * r; }`?
questions.explanation: A prototype lists the return type, name, and parameter *types*, terminated by a semicolon. Names are optional. Option D is a definition (not a prototype).

questions.stem:
The function below is intended to set both `a` and `b` to zero. Which version works?
```cpp
// Goal: after the call, x == 0 and y == 0 in the caller.
```

options.text: `void zero(int a, int b) { a = 0; b = 0; }`

questions.explanation: To modify the caller's variables, the function must receive references or pointers. Pointers (B) work when called as `zero(&x, &y);`. Equivalent reference version: `void zero(int& a, int& b)`.
C++ allows **default arguments**. Missing arguments at the call are filled in from right to left using the defaults declared in the function signature.

options.text: C++ permits **function overloading** — same name, different parameter types
The two functions have different return types, so they are distinct
The compiler renames the second function automatically

questions.explanation: C++ allows multiple functions with the same name as long as their **parameter lists differ** (different number or types). The compiler picks the right one based on the argument types at the call site. Return types alone are not enough to overload.

questions.stem: Which call would the compiler reject for `int sum(int, int);`?
questions.explanation: The number of arguments at the call must match the number of formal parameters (unless defaults are declared). Type mismatches like B trigger an implicit conversion (often with a warning), but a wrong **count** is always a hard error.

options.text: `100 5` — the function uses the global, `main` uses its local
`5 100` — the function uses the most recent assignment

questions.explanation: Each function looks up names in **its own scope** first, then globals. `show()` has no local `a`, so it finds the global `100`. `main` has its own `a = 5`, which shadows the global *only inside `main`*.

questions.stem: Which is the **best style** when a function only reads its argument and never modifies it, and the argument is a small built-in type like `int`?

options.text: Pass by const reference: `void f(const int& x)`

questions.explanation: For small built-in types (`int`, `char`, `float`, `double`), pass-by-value is **simplest and equally fast** — the copy is essentially free. Const-reference is preferred for **large** objects (strings, structs, vectors) where copying is expensive.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a **Type 1** function (no arguments, no return value)?

options.text: Useful for printing a banner or menu
Useful for computing a math result
Useful for receiving user input and returning it
Cannot exist — every function must return something

questions.explanation: A void function with no parameters is ideal for **side-effect-only** actions such as printing a fixed banner or menu. Its signature looks like `void greet();`.

questions.stem:
Identify the type:
```cpp
void printSquare(int n) { cout << n*n; }
```
questions.explanation: The function receives an `int` argument but its return type is `void`. It performs an action (printing) without returning a value.

questions.stem: In the call `add(x, y)`, the names `x` and `y` are called the:
questions.explanation: **Actual arguments** appear in the function call (the *actual* values passed). **Formal arguments** appear in the function definition's parameter list (placeholders that *receive* the values).

questions.stem: What must match between actual and formal arguments?
questions.explanation: The compiler matches arguments by **position**, so the order, number, and type must all be consistent. The names need not match — `add(x, y)` calling `int add(int a, int b)` works fine.
Each call to `modify()` adds 5 to the global `x`. After two calls, `x = 10 + 5 + 5 = 20`.

questions.stem: A global variable in C++ is **automatically initialised to**:

options.text: The value of the previous global with the same name

questions.explanation: Globals (and `static` locals) are zero-initialised by default. Only **non-static local** variables of built-in types start with garbage if not explicitly initialised.

options.text: `cout << k;` — `k` is local to `f` and is not visible in `main`

questions.explanation: `k` is a local variable inside `f()`. It exists only during the execution of `f` and is **invisible** outside it. Trying to use `k` in `main` is a scope error.

questions.stem: Identify the **two essential components** every recursive function must have.

options.text: A base case and a recursive case
A global variable and a parameter

questions.explanation: A **base case** stops the recursion, and a **recursive case** moves the problem closer to the base case. Without a base case, recursion never stops and causes a stack overflow.
The base case `n <= 1` covers both `n = 0` and `n = 1`, returning `1`. Mathematically, `0! = 1`.

questions.stem: What happens if you remove the base case from a recursive function?

options.text: The function still works, just slower
The compiler refuses to compile it
The function calls itself indefinitely until a stack overflow

questions.explanation: Without a base case, every call makes another call. The call stack grows until memory runs out — a **stack overflow** crash.

options.text: `for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) total += i;`
`for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) total += n;`
`for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) total = i;`

questions.explanation: Add each integer from 1 to `n` to the running total. Option B adds `n` to itself `n` times (giving `n*n`). Option C and D are buggy.
`b^e = b × b^(e-1)`, with base case `b^0 = 1`. Option A never reduces `e`, so it never reaches the base case.

questions.stem: What is the maximum recursion depth (number of simultaneously active stack frames) when computing `factorial(5)` with the standard `if (n <= 1) return 1;` base case?
questions.explanation: Active frames at the deepest point: `factorial(5)`, `factorial(4)`, `factorial(3)`, `factorial(2)`, `factorial(1)` — five frames. `factorial(1)` hits the base case and returns immediately without spawning another call.

questions.stem: Why is iteration usually preferred over recursion for **simple sequential** tasks?

options.text: Iteration is more readable for repetition without recursive structure
Iteration cannot be implemented in C++
Recursion always crashes on inputs above 10

questions.explanation: Loops avoid the per-call stack overhead and are more idiomatic for problems that lack a natural recursive structure (like adding 1..n). Recursion shines for problems with a self-similar shape (trees, divide-and-conquer).
Inside `f`, the local `x = 2` shadows the global, so `f` prints `2`. `g` has no local `x`, so it modifies the **global** `x` to `3` and prints `3`. `main` then prints the global, which is now `3`.

questions.stem: Which is a **safer alternative** to a global variable for sharing data between two functions?

options.text: Pass it explicitly as a parameter and/or return value
Re-declare it in each function as `extern`
Use the same name in both functions to make it global automatically

questions.explanation: Passing data through parameters and return values keeps each function **self-contained**, easier to test, and free of hidden coupling. Globals work but increase coupling and make bugs harder to track.
Every call to `inc()` increases the global `counter` by 1. The loop runs 4 times → final value `4`.
There is no `if` statement to stop the recursion. Every call spawns another call → stack overflow. Add `if (n <= 1) return 1;` at the top.

questions.stem: The Fibonacci sequence is `0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...` Which recursive definition matches `fib(n)` for this sequence?
questions.explanation: Two base cases (`fib(0) = 0`, `fib(1) = 1`) and the recurrence `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` for `n >= 2`.
`fib(6)` evaluates to `8`. Sequence: `0,1,1,2,3,5,8` — the 7th term (index 6) is `8`.

questions.stem: Which function is the more efficient way to compute `n!` for **large `n`**, given that recursion uses O(n) extra stack space?

options.text: The iterative version using a `for` loop

questions.explanation: The iterative version uses O(1) extra space (a single accumulator) regardless of `n`. Recursion uses O(n) stack space, risking overflow for huge `n`.

questions.stem: In the function `int average(int x, int y)` called as `average(p, q)`:

options.text: `x` and `y` are actual arguments; `p` and `q` are formal arguments
`p` and `q` are actual arguments; `x` and `y` are formal arguments
`p`, `q`, `x`, `y` are all references to the same variables

questions.explanation: Definitions hold **formal** parameters; calls supply **actual** arguments. Mnemonic: *Formal = in the Function (definition); Actual = at the call*.

questions.stem: What is a key difference between **local** and **global** variables?

options.text: Local variables persist across function calls; globals do not
Locals exist only during their block's execution; globals last for the whole program
Locals are automatically zero-initialised; globals are not

questions.explanation: Locals live on the stack for the duration of their block; globals live in the data segment for the lifetime of the program. Default-initialisation is the reverse of (C): **globals** are zero-initialised, **locals** are not.

questions.stem: Choose the **best signature** for a function that returns whether a year is a leap year.
questions.explanation: Returning `bool` makes the function self-documenting and works directly with `if`. The `is...` naming convention also makes the call site read like English: `if (isLeapYear(2024)) ...`.

questions.stem: Complete the body of `bool isLeapYear(int y)`:
questions.explanation: The Gregorian rule: divisible by 4 but **not** by 100, **unless** also divisible by 400. Examples: 2000 (leap), 1900 (not leap), 2024 (leap), 2100 (not leap).
Each call adds `2` and reduces `n` by 1 until `n == 0` returns 0. Total `2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 0 = 8`. (This computes `2n`.)
The base case only fires at `n == 1`. For `n = 0` (or any negative input), the recursion never stops. A safer base case is `if (n <= 0) return 0;`.
Each call doubles `x`. Starting from 10: → 20 → 40 → **80**.

questions.stem: Which mathematical series does the chapter's `series` example approximate?
questions.explanation: The series `x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − x⁷/7! + …` is the Taylor expansion of **sin(x)**. The chapter verifies the result by comparing against `sin(x)` from `<cmath>`.

questions.stem: What is an array, in one sentence?

options.text: A pointer to a single value of any type
A collection of *different* data types stored in contiguous memory
A consecutive group of *homogeneous* memory locations sharing one name
An object with named members accessed by the dot operator

questions.explanation: Arrays are contiguous, fixed-size, homogeneous (same type for every element). Heterogeneous types belong to a `struct`; named-member access is also a struct feature.

questions.stem: What is the value of `arr[3]` after `int arr[6] = {10, 20, 30};`?
questions.explanation: When fewer initialisers are given than the declared size, the **remaining elements are zero-initialised**. So `arr` = `{10, 20, 30, 0, 0, 0}`.

questions.stem: The shortcut `int arr[100] = {0};` initialises:

options.text: Only the first element to 0; the rest are garbage

questions.explanation: The first element is explicitly `0`, and the partial-initialisation rule sets every other element to `0` as well.

questions.stem: What is the index of the **last** element of `int arr[10];`?
questions.explanation: Indices run from `0` to `size − 1`. For a size-10 array, valid indices are `0..9`.

questions.stem: What happens when you read or write `arr[10]` in a 10-element array?

options.text: Compile error — array index out of range
Undefined behaviour: anything from garbage to a crash to silent memory corruption

questions.explanation: C++ does **no bounds checking** on raw arrays. Out-of-range access is undefined behaviour and may corrupt nearby memory or crash unpredictably.
Replace `maxVal` whenever a **larger** element appears. Option A would compute the *minimum*. Option C just stores the last element.
The loop walks the array backwards from index 4 to 0, printing the elements in reverse order. The loop stops when `i` becomes `-1` because `-1 >= 0` is false.
Increment only when the element matches. Option C uses `=` (assignment), which silently overwrites and is almost certainly a bug.

questions.stem: The `search` function on page 28 of the chapter returns:

options.text: The **index** of `x`, or `-1` if not found

questions.explanation: Linear search returns the position (index) of the first occurrence, or `-1` (a sentinel value) when the target is missing.

questions.stem: What does the linear-search algorithm have **time complexity**?
questions.explanation: In the worst case, every element is examined → O(n). Binary search achieves O(log n) but only on **sorted** arrays.

options.text: The loop reads `a[1]..a[5]`, but valid indices are `0..4`. `a[0]` is skipped and `a[5]` is out of bounds.
The array must be initialised first

questions.explanation: Off-by-one error — a classic. The correct loop is `for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)`.
`a[0]+a[1] = 1+2 = 3`, so we print `a[3]` which is `4`.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a **valid** array declaration in standard C++?
questions.explanation: The size must be a compile-time constant (or deducible from an initialiser list). Variable-length arrays (A) are a GCC extension, not standard C++. (B) is illegal because the compiler cannot determine the size.

questions.stem: Two arrays where parallel index positions correspond to a single conceptual record (e.g., `name[i]` and `age[i]`) are called:
questions.explanation: **Parallel arrays** are a simple way to associate multiple attributes per record before learning structures.
The first loop doubles every element. The second prints the result.

questions.stem: Complete the body of `int sum(int a[], int n)`:

options.text: `for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) s += a[i]; return s;`
`for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += a[i]; return s;`        *(with `int s = 0;` first)*
`for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) s += a[i]; return s;`

questions.explanation: Iterate over `0..n−1`, accumulating into `s`. (A) would read `a[n]` (out of bounds). (C) skips `a[0]`. (D) only sums two elements.

questions.stem:
Why does the function below behave as if **the array were passed by reference**, even though it looks like an ordinary parameter?
```cpp
void zeroOut(int a[], int n) { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] = 0; }
```

options.text: Array names decay to **pointers** when passed to a function — the function operates on the original memory
Functions cannot modify their parameters at all
The compiler always passes by reference

questions.explanation: When you pass an array, C++ passes a **pointer to its first element**. Modifying `a[i]` inside the function modifies the original array.

questions.stem: Inside `void f(int a[])`, what does `sizeof(a)` return?

options.text: The number of elements in the array
The total bytes occupied by the array
The size of a **pointer** (typically 4 or 8 bytes), not the array

questions.explanation: Inside the function, `a` is a pointer, so `sizeof(a)` gives the pointer's size, not the array's. To know the array length, **pass it as a separate parameter** (`int n`).

`sizeof(a)` is the total bytes (`6 * sizeof(int) = 24`), and `sizeof(a[0])` is the size of one element (`4`). So `n = 24/4 = 6`. *Note: this trick only works in the **same scope** where the array is declared, not inside a function that received it.

questions.stem: Implement a one-line **swap of two array elements**:

options.text: `int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t;`        *(three statements, not one)*

questions.explanation: The standard library's `std::swap(a[i], a[j])` is the cleanest one-liner. Option B is the manual three-line approach. Option A overwrites and loses data.

questions.stem: Which describes the result of `int a[5] = {1, 2};`?
questions.explanation: The first two elements take the listed values; the remaining elements are zero-initialised.
`b[i]` receives `a[4 - i]` — the array is copied **in reverse**.
Use a separate counter for each output array, and **increment** it after each insertion. Option C overwrites position 0 every iteration. Option A uses the source index (could leave gaps).
Walks the array; the smallest value is `1` at index `4`. (Tracking the **index** as well as the value is a useful pattern.)

questions.stem: Which is the cleanest way to **reverse an array in place** with `n` elements?

options.text: Copy to a new array, then back, in reverse
Sort the array in descending order

questions.explanation: Swap symmetric pairs. Only `n/2` swaps are needed. (C) is wrong because reverse ≠ sorted unless the array is already sorted.
Print only odd elements (`a[i] % 2 == 1`). The odd elements are `15` and `23`.

questions.stem: Suppose `int a[] = {3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5};`. How many times does `5` appear?
questions.explanation: The value `5` appears at indices 4, 8, and 10 → three occurrences. (Counting occurrences is a one-liner with a `for` and an `if`.)

questions.stem:
What is the issue with `int a[]` (no size, no initialiser)?
```cpp
int a[];
```

options.text: The compiler defaults the size to 1
The compiler reports an error: incomplete type / unknown size

questions.explanation: Without an initialiser the compiler cannot determine the array length, so the declaration is rejected.

questions.stem: The chapter's `search` function returns `-1` to indicate "not found". This is an example of:

options.text: An error code returned through a special integer value (a **sentinel**)

questions.explanation: Returning a value that cannot be a valid result (here, `-1`, since indices are non-negative) is a classic C-style way to signal failure. Modern alternatives include exceptions and `std::optional`.

questions.stem: How many elements does `int m[3][4]` contain?
questions.explanation: `rows * cols = 3 * 4 = 12`. Total bytes are `12 * sizeof(int)` (typically 48 bytes).

questions.stem: Which declaration is **invalid**?
questions.explanation: The **column size cannot be omitted**. Only the row count can be deduced because the compiler must know how many elements are in each row to lay them out.
Row index `1` (second row) and column index `2` (third column) → `6`.

questions.stem: In **row-major** memory layout, the element after `m[i][j]` in memory is:
questions.explanation: Row-major means an entire row is laid out before the next row begins, so consecutive memory addresses correspond to consecutive **column indices** in the same row.

questions.stem: Which loop pair correctly **reads** a 3 × 4 array `arr` from `cin`?
questions.explanation: The outer loop iterates over rows (size 3) and the inner loop over columns (size 4). Option A swaps the bounds and goes out of range on the rows.

questions.stem: For an `n × n` matrix, the **main-diagonal** elements are those where:
questions.explanation: Main diagonal: row index equals column index. The condition `i + j == n − 1` describes the *secondary* diagonal.

questions.stem: For a 4 × 4 matrix, which positions are on the **secondary diagonal**?
questions.explanation: `i + j == 3` → indices `(0,3), (1,2), (2,1), (3,0)`. (A) is the main diagonal; (C) is the four corners.
Main diagonal: `m[i][i]`. Option A sums the first row. Option B sums the first column. Option D sums the secondary diagonal.

questions.stem: Complete the line that **sums the secondary diagonal**:
questions.explanation: The column index for row `i` on the secondary diagonal is `n - 1 - i`. (B) overshoots by one.

questions.stem: For an `n × n` matrix, the elements **above the main diagonal** (the upper triangle) satisfy:
questions.explanation: Upper triangle: row index is **less** than column index. Lower triangle: `i > j`.
Main-diagonal sum: `1 + 5 + 9 = 15`.
Secondary-diagonal sum for a 3 × 3: `m[0][2]+m[1][1]+m[2][0] = 3 + 5 + 7 = 15`. (For this magic-like matrix, both diagonals happen to sum to the same value.)
The element at row `i`, column `j` lands at index `i * C + j` in row-major flat layout. (D) would be column-major.

questions.stem: To compute the **sum of each column** of an `R × C` matrix, you should:

options.text: Reset the accumulator inside the row loop
Reset the accumulator inside the column loop, with the row loop on the inside
Use a single loop over the diagonals
Use one accumulator for the whole matrix

questions.explanation: For column sums, the **outer loop runs over columns** (`j`), the inner loop walks **down the rows** (`i`), and the accumulator resets at the start of each column.

questions.stem: The chapter notes that for a matrix with an **odd** dimension, the centre element belongs to:
questions.explanation: For a 3×3 matrix, position `(1,1)` satisfies `i == j` (main) and `i + j == n − 1 = 2` (secondary). To avoid double-counting in the combined sum, subtract that element once.

questions.stem: Replace every `5` in a 2D array with `0`. Which fragment is correct?
questions.explanation: Use `==` for comparison. (A) uses `=` (assignment), which sets the element to 5 and is non-zero (true), so the body always runs. (C) is malformed ternary syntax. (D) overwrites everything.

questions.stem: Which loop initialises an `n × n` matrix to the **identity matrix** (1s on the main diagonal, 0s elsewhere)?
questions.explanation: For each cell, store `1` if on the main diagonal, otherwise `0`. (C) only sets the diagonal but doesn't zero out the rest, so the matrix is left full of garbage (or whatever it had before).

questions.stem: The most efficient way to set just the diagonal (assuming the matrix is already zero) is:

options.text: One loop: `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) m[i][i] = 1;`

questions.explanation: A single linear loop visits exactly the `n` diagonal cells — O(n) instead of O(n²).
The sum of the main diagonal of an identity matrix equals its dimension. This sum is called the **trace** of the matrix.

questions.stem: To **transpose** a matrix means to:
questions.explanation: The transpose flips a matrix over its main diagonal. A 2 × 3 matrix becomes 3 × 2.
Element at `(i,j)` in the original goes to `(j,i)` in the transpose.

options.text: The number of elements on the main diagonal
The number of elements **strictly below** the main diagonal
The number of elements on the secondary diagonal

questions.explanation: `i > j` defines the **strict lower triangle**. For a 4 × 4 matrix it has `n(n−1)/2 = 6` elements.

questions.stem: To read a 2D matrix declared as `int m[R][C]` and pass it to a function, the function must declare:

options.text: `void f(int m[][C], int R)`        *(column size required)*

questions.explanation: When an array is passed, only the **leftmost** dimension can be omitted. The compiler needs the column count to compute the address `m[i][j] = base + i * C + j`.

questions.stem: To print a 3 × 3 matrix in **column-major** order (column by column), the loop nesting is:

options.text: A single loop with index `i*3 + j`

questions.explanation: To visit cells column by column, put the column loop on the **outside** and step rows on the inside.

questions.stem: What is the result of multiplying a 2 × 3 matrix by a 3 × 4 matrix?
questions.explanation: For matrix product `A × B`, A's columns must equal B's rows. The result has A's rows and B's columns: 2 × 4.
The dot product of row `i` of A with column `j` of B accumulates into `c[i][j]`.

options.text: Off-by-one — `i` reaches `3`, so `m[3][j]` writes outside the array

questions.explanation: `i <= 3` runs for `i = 0,1,2,3`. When `i = 3`, `m[3][j]` is out of bounds (valid rows are 0..2). C++ will not catch this; expect undefined behaviour.

questions.stem: A C-style string is stored as:

options.text: An array of characters terminated by `'\0'`
A pointer to a single character

questions.explanation: C-strings are arrays of `char` ending in the **null terminator** `'\0'`. The terminator tells library functions where the string ends.

questions.stem: The string literal `"ABCD"` occupies how many bytes (assuming `sizeof(char) == 1`)?
questions.explanation: Four visible characters plus one byte for the terminating `'\0'` → 5 bytes total.

questions.stem: Which declaration is **too small** to hold the string `"Mazin Alaa"`?
questions.explanation: `"Mazin Alaa"` has 10 visible characters, so the array must hold at least 11 chars (10 + null terminator). `char s[10]` would be one byte short.

questions.stem: What does `strlen("Hello")` return?
questions.explanation: `strlen` counts **visible** characters — it does **not** include the null terminator.

questions.stem: To read a sentence with spaces into `char s[100]`, you should use:
questions.explanation: `>>` stops at whitespace, so it cannot read a full sentence. `cin.getline(s, 100)` reads up to 99 characters or until newline. `gets` is dangerous and removed.
The loop walks character by character and stops when it finds `'\0'`, printing `Hello`. The terminator itself is not printed.

questions.stem: After `char a[10] = "abc";`, what does `strlen(a)` return and what does `sizeof(a)` return?
questions.explanation: `strlen` counts visible chars (3). `sizeof` is the **storage size** of the array (10 bytes), independent of contents.

questions.stem: Which header provides `strlen`, `strcpy`, `strcat`, `strcmp`?
questions.explanation: `<cstring>` is the C++ wrapper for the C `<string.h>`. `<string>` is for the **C++** `std::string` class.

questions.stem: After `char a[20] = "abcd"; char b[] = "1234"; strcat(a, b);`, what is `a`?
questions.explanation: `strcat` **appends** the second argument to the first. The destination `a` must have enough room (here, 20 chars is plenty).

options.text: `a` only has room for `"abcd\0"`; appending `"1234"` writes past its end → **buffer overflow**
`a` and `b` must be the same size

questions.explanation: After concatenation, `a` would need to hold `"abcd1234\0"` = 9 bytes, but only 5 were allocated. The extra characters spill into adjacent memory — undefined behaviour, possibly a crash or security hole.

questions.stem: What does `strcmp(s1, s2)` return when the two strings are **equal**?
questions.explanation: Equal strings → `0`. Positive → `s1 > s2`, negative → `s1 < s2`. Comparison is lexicographic, character by character.
`'a' < 'b'`, so `apple` comes before `banana` lexicographically. `strcmp` returns negative, so the `if` body runs.

questions.stem:
What's wrong?
```cpp
char a[20] = "Hello", b[20] = "World";
a = b;          // intend: assign b's content to a
```

options.text: Array names are not assignable; use `strcpy(a, b);` instead
The arrays must have the same size

questions.explanation: C-style arrays cannot be assigned with `=`. Use `strcpy(a, b)` or `std::string`.

questions.stem: Which converts `"123"` to the integer `123`?
questions.explanation: `atoi` (ASCII to int) parses a numeric string. (B) returns 3 (length). Modern alternative: `std::stoi("123")`.

questions.stem: Which converts `"3.14"` to a `double`?
questions.explanation: `atof` (ASCII to floating-point) parses a decimal string into a `double`. Modern alternative: `std::stod`.

questions.stem: Why might `itoa` not compile on your machine?
questions.explanation: `itoa` is **not** part of the C or C++ standard. Use `sprintf(buf, "%d", n)` or `std::to_string(n)` (C++11) for portability.
Strings declared as `char[]` are mutable: replacing index 1 (`'b'`) with `'X'` yields `"aXc"`. Note: a `const char* p = "abc"` literal is **not** writable.

questions.stem: Convert all characters of `char s[100]` to **uppercase** in one line. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: `toupper` operates on a single `char`. Loop through the string until `'\0'`. (B) and (C) and (D) treat the array as a single value, which doesn't work.

questions.stem: After `char buf[10]; for (int i=0;i<5;i++) buf[i] = 'A' + i;`, calling `cout << buf;` may print:

options.text: `ABCDE` followed by **garbage**, until a `'\0'` happens to appear

questions.explanation: The loop fills 5 characters but **never appends `'\0'`**. `cout << buf;` keeps printing past index 4 until it encounters a zero byte. Always terminate manually: `buf[5] = '\0';`.

questions.stem: Which one-line snippet **correctly** copies `src` into `dst` *and* appends a null terminator?

options.text: `for (int i = 0; src[i]; i++) dst[i] = src[i];`        *(forgets the `'\0'`)*

questions.explanation: `strcpy` copies up to and **including** the `'\0'`. Option B copies the visible chars but stops before the terminator, leaving `dst` un-terminated.
`strlen` ignores `'\0'` → 11 visible chars. `sizeof(s)` includes the terminator → 12 bytes.

questions.stem: The character `'\0'` has ASCII value:
questions.explanation: `'\0'` is the **null** character — ASCII value `0`. Don't confuse it with the digit `'0'` (ASCII 48).

questions.stem: Implement `bool isEmpty(char *s)` that returns whether the string has length 0.
questions.explanation: An empty C-string starts with `'\0'`. (A) checks for a null pointer (different concept). (C) checks for length 1. (D) compares pointers, not contents.

questions.stem: Reverse a C-string in place, given its length `n`. Which fragment works?

options.text: `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) swap(s[i], s[n - 1 - i]);`        *(swaps twice — no net change)*
`for (int i = 0; i < n / 2; i++) swap(s[i], s[n - 1 - i]);`
`for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s[i] = s[n - i];`
`for (int i = n; i >= 0; i--) s[i] = s[i + 1];`

questions.explanation: Swap symmetric pairs only **half** the length, otherwise each swap is undone. (A) restores the original. (C) and (D) don't reverse correctly and may go out of bounds.
After comparing the common prefix "abc" equally, `a` ends (`'\0'`) while `b` has another character. `'\0' < 'd'`, so `a` is "less than" `b`. The conditional prints `shorter`.

questions.stem: Which sentence about `cin.ignore(80, '\n');` is true?

options.text: It deletes the next 80 lines of input
It discards up to 80 characters or until a newline, whichever comes first

questions.explanation: `ignore` is the standard way to flush leftover input (typically the newline left after `cin >> n`) before a `getline` call.

questions.stem: The expression `cout.put('A');` is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: `cout.put(c)` writes a single character — same effect as either `<<`-based form for a single character.

questions.stem: Why is `std::string` (from `<string>`) usually preferred over C-style strings in modern C++?

options.text: It manages its own memory, supports `+`, `==`, and dynamic resizing
It is faster on every operation
C-style strings are illegal in C++

questions.explanation: `std::string` removes manual size and `'\0'` management, supports natural operators, and grows automatically — eliminating an entire class of buffer-overflow bugs.
The letter `l` appears twice in `"Hello"`.
After concatenation: `"Hello World"` → 11 visible characters (5 + 1 space + 5).

questions.stem: What is a `struct` in C++?

options.text: A grouping of named members of (possibly) **different** data types
A fixed-size array of one type
A function that returns multiple values

questions.explanation: A `struct` bundles related data of varying types under one name. Arrays bundle items of the **same** type.

questions.stem: The closing brace of a `struct` definition is followed by:
questions.explanation: `struct Name { ... };` — forgetting the semicolon is one of the most common compile errors.

questions.stem: Which is the correct way to access the `age` member of a `Student s;`?
questions.explanation: The **dot operator** is used on struct *variables*. The arrow `->` is for **pointers** to structs (`Student* p; p->age;`).
Brace initialisation assigns `x = 3`, `y = 4` in declaration order. Sum = 7.

questions.stem:
Which line is invalid?
```cpp
struct Point { int x, y; };
Point a = {1, 2};
Point b = a;          // line 1
b.x = 10;             // line 2
a = b;                 // line 3
a.x + b.x;             // line 4
```

options.text: line 4 — actually all four are valid

questions.explanation: Structs **can** be copied member-wise with `=` (unlike C-style arrays). All four lines compile and behave intuitively.

questions.stem: Which is **not** a valid way to declare a struct variable?

options.text: `typedef struct { int x; } Data; Data d;`

questions.explanation: The struct must be **defined before** any variable of that type is declared.
Chain dot operators to descend into nested structs.
`P y = x;` performs a **copy**, so `y` is independent. Modifying `y.a` does not affect `x.a`.

questions.stem: What is the size of `struct S { char c; int i; };` on a typical 64-bit system?
questions.explanation: The compiler adds **padding** between `char c` and `int i` so that `int i` starts on a 4-byte boundary. Total: 1 + 3 padding + 4 = **8** bytes.

questions.stem: Which is true of an **array of structures** like `Student arr[10];`?

options.text: All 10 elements share the same members' memory
Each element is a complete struct with its own copies of all members
The members must all be of the same primitive type

questions.explanation: An array of structs is just an array — each cell is a full struct. Access: `arr[i].member`.
Index 1 is the second struct, whose `msg` is `"NotFound"`.

questions.stem: Which is the typedef syntax that lets you write `Student s;` instead of `struct Student s;`?
questions.explanation: `typedef struct { ... } Alias;` creates an alias. (Note: in **C++**, simply writing `struct Student { int age; };` already lets you write `Student s;` — `typedef` is mostly a C carry-over.)

questions.stem: To pass a struct **without copying it** so the function can modify it, declare:

options.text: `void f(Student& s)`            *(by reference — no copy, modifies caller)*
`void f(Student* s)`            *(by pointer — also no copy)*

questions.explanation: Reference and pointer parameters both avoid copying and allow modification. Reference is more idiomatic in modern C++; pointer is necessary when the argument can be `nullptr`.

questions.stem: To accept a struct without copying but **prevent modification**, use:
questions.explanation: `const Student&` gives the speed of pass-by-reference and the safety of read-only access. This is the standard C++ idiom for large read-only inputs.

questions.stem: Through a pointer, struct members are accessed using:
questions.explanation: `p->member` is shorthand for `(*p).member`.
`p->y` is the second member, `2`.

questions.stem: A struct containing a `char name[30];` member uses how many bytes for the name field?

options.text: 30 always (regardless of the actual string length)
The length of the stored string + 1
0 bytes if the name is empty

questions.explanation: Storage is fixed by the array declaration. `strlen(s.name)` may be small, but the struct still reserves all 30 bytes.

questions.stem:
The struct below is intended to model a 2D point. Which constructor-style initialisation works in C++11+?
```cpp
struct Point { double x, y; };
```
questions.explanation: Aggregate initialisation with braces sets each member in declaration order.

questions.stem: Which is the **biggest difference** between `struct` and `class` in C++?

options.text: `struct` cannot have member functions, but `class` can
Default access in `struct` is **public**; default in `class` is **private**
There is no difference at all

questions.explanation: Both can have members and methods. The only real difference is the **default access specifier** and default inheritance access. Convention: use `struct` for plain data aggregates and `class` for objects with invariants.
`area` returns `w * h` = `3 * 4 = 12`. The struct is passed by value (a small copy is fine here).

questions.stem: To **return** a struct from a function, the return type is:

options.text: A pointer to a static struct

questions.explanation: Functions can return structs by value just like any other type. (B) and (C) are older C-era patterns that are rarely needed in modern C++.

questions.stem: Add 1 inch carry-over: feet = 5, inches = 11.5, plus inches = 0.7. What does the chapter's `distance` example produce?
questions.explanation: Total inches = 12.2. Since 12.2 ≥ 12, subtract 12 (→ 0.2) and add 1 to feet (→ 6). Result: 6 feet, 0.2 inches.

questions.stem: Implement `bool equal(Point a, Point b)` for a 2D point. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Compare member by member. Aggregate `==` is auto-generated only in C++20 (`= default`); in earlier standards you must write the comparison yourself.
`S u({3, 4});` is not standard aggregate-initialisation syntax. Use `S u = {3, 4};` or `S u{3, 4};`. The other lines are all valid.

questions.stem: To group a student's name (string), age (int), and GPA (float), the **most natural** choice is:
questions.explanation: A struct keeps related fields together as one logical record, and an `array of struct` is the natural extension to many students.
C++11 supports **default member initialisers**. `n = 0` inside the struct sets the default, so any new `Count` has `n = 0` automatically.
Element-wise vector add: `c.dx = 1 + 3 = 4`, `c.dy = 2 + 4 = 6`.

questions.stem: Which sentence is **true**?

options.text: Two structs of the same shape are interchangeable types
Each struct definition introduces a **distinct** type, even if the members match
`struct A { int x; };` and `struct B { int x; };` define the same type
Structs cannot be parameters of functions

questions.explanation: `struct A` and `struct B` are different types even with identical members. To convert, you must copy member-by-member or use a common type.

questions.stem: To find the student with the **highest GPA** in `Student arr[N]`, the cleanest pattern is:

options.text: Sort the array, then take the first element
Track an index `bestIdx = 0; for (i=1..N-1) if (arr[i].gpa > arr[bestIdx].gpa) bestIdx = i;`
Use recursion with the array as a global

questions.explanation: Linear scan with an index of the current best — O(n), in-place, no extra memory. Sorting (A) works but is O(n log n), unnecessary if you only need the max.
